title: Theo and the Fake Tapestry
markdown:
Theo, an expert on old things, adjusted his glasses. His car, which smelled of polish and old books, sat outside the fancy gates of Ages & Ages Past. This was not a normal park. History was not merely remembered here; it was acted out, often with too much sparkle. Theo had come to check a tapestry people said was very old, or at least that was the claim.

In the courtyard a blur of colour and loud energy rushed at him: Lucia, the park’s historian, who loved stories so much she sometimes forgot what was true.

“Mr. Theo. Welcome.” Her voice was bubbly, dark curls bouncing, eyes bright. “You’ve come for the Chronos Cloth. It’s amazing. A whisper from the beginning of time, threads of pure legend.”

Theo gave a small quiet nod. He had heard whispers before. Usually they were not very true.

The tapestry hung in the Hall of Ages, among old wax, dusty velvet, and a hint of desperation from whoever wrote the advertisements. It showed a dragon with bright red scales, very angry, chasing a knight whose armour shone with a gleam that seemed too good to be true. The park’s boss, Bartholomew Featherbottom III, beamed. His special eyeglass kept wanting to fall off.

“This,” Bartholomew announced, puffing his chest, “is the Dragon-Slayer’s Shroud. Woven by the famous Sir Reginald himself in 783. He fought the Serpent of the Whispering Peaks. A true tale of bravery.”

Theo made a low sound that meant hard thinking, or a funny stomach. His long fingers touched a bright stitch on the dragon’s wing.

“Interesting. And what about the other story that came with it?”

Bartholomew looked confused, as if he had lost a piece of costume. “Other story? My dear fellow, there’s only the story. The one that’s absolutely, totally, historically real.”

Lucia stepped closer, playful. “Actually,” she whispered, “our research also says it was a gift. Woven by Princess Aurelia for her secret love, a handsome blacksmith, before a dangerous journey. She put wishes into it for his safety. That’s why the dragon looks so upset.” She winked. “The third story says it was a badly written shopping list. A grumpy baker wrote it in an old language. It shows how mad he was about dough that wouldn’t stop growing.”

Theo blinked. Dragon-Slayer’s Shroud, love gift, or baker’s complaint? His eyebrows twitched. He looked closer. The colours were too bright for something nearly twelve hundred years old; they had a modern pop. Then his eyes found a tiny tag near the bottom, hidden under a dragon’s claw. Small letters: Ages & Ages Past – Original Collection – Made in 2019. Quality Assured.

A rumble started in Theo’s chest, the sound before a well-aimed dart. A strong gust, probably from a robot knight fighting outside, caught a big fake cannon Bartholomew had placed in the room. With a bang and a puff of smoke it fired. No cannonball: a shower of colourful confetti, sticking to the tapestry’s modern threads like a strange happy snowstorm.

Bartholomew yelped like a small dog out of treats. Lucia gasped, minty breath catching, sparkle dimming. Theo, calm through the storm, picked a blue piece off the cloth.

“I see,” he said, quiet, carrying the weight of many careful checks. “So the Chronos Cloth is not really old, but more like a picture that tells a story.”

Lucia’s shoulders drooped. The trick was over. Bright threads, different stories, confetti bomb: made-up fun and acting. She looked at Theo, energy now a soft glow.

“It was meant to be special,” she mumbled. “People like big stories. They want to believe in dragons and knights and true love. I just made them a little bigger.”

Theo looked at her earnest face, then at the confetti-covered tapestry, planned grandeur mixed with silly mistakes. He imagined how happy it made visitors, even if it was not real.

“Lucia, being truthful is important. But so is using your imagination. Maybe this tapestry isn’t the Dragon-Slayer’s Shroud, or a princess’s wish, or a baker’s complaint. In its own way it shows how powerful stories are. You are a very good storyteller. You just need to learn that the most wonderful tales are the ones that are true, or are shared honestly, with a little sparkle.”

He turned to Bartholomew, who was still wiping confetti from his eyeglass.

“Mr. Featherbottom, this tapestry is a wonderful piece of art, made with skill to spark imagination. Its specialness comes not from its age but from the passion put into it. It is, really, a story told very well.”

And so the Chronos Cloth found its true story: not ancient, still full of wonder, and a reminder that tales, real or imagined, want honesty as much as flair.
characters: Theo (an antique appraiser), Lucia (the heritage-park historian)
